documents.text:
Pre-Conference Joint Comments of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation
                            and the Western Electricity Coordinating Council

                                  2026 Reliability Technical Conference
                           United States Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
                                          Docket No. AD26-8-000
                                            October 21, 2026


The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) and the Western Electricity Coordinating Council
(WECC) are pleased to submit joint pre-conference comments for the 2026 Reliability Technical Conference.
These comments are divided into three parts: an overview of bulk power system (BPS) reliability in North
America, and separate discussions of topics identified for panels one and two.

BPS Reliability in North America
By many objective measures, the North American bulk power system remains highly reliable, while significant
new and intensifying risks challenge our ability to sustain that performance. These risks include extreme
weather, a rapidly changing generation resource mix, unprecedented rising demand for electricity, and
cybersecurity threats. The result is a system that is running closer to the edge, with higher amounts of
inverter-based loads and generation, with increased reliance on extraordinary industry actions, leaving less
room for error.

NERC’s 2026 State of Reliability (SOR) finds that the bulk power system remained highly reliable and resilient
in 2025. Notable points include strong transmission performance, frequency response improvements in the
Eastern, Western, and Texas Interconnections, and stable protection system misoperations at a historically
low rate. There were ten Level 3 Energy Emergency Alerts (EEAs) in 2025, down from 21 in 2024. None
included operator-initiated firm load shedding. During the severe eastern heat of June and July, system
operators declared 20 EEAs yet managed high loading without shedding firm load. During the most
challenging winter week, January 19 through 25, 2025, performance improved relative to earlier severe
winter events. Additional generator commitments, better preparedness and situational awareness,
continued winterization, and implementation of lessons learned from prior storms contributed to positive
performance. NERC’s enhanced cold weather standards underpin these improvements.

Reliable performance demonstrates extraordinary preparation, coordination, and real-time mitigation by
industry. However, extensive use of EEAs shows a system operating under tighter constraints with greater
dependence on operator intervention – a scenario that should not be normalized. Underlying conditions
reveal the key drivers of risk:

    •   Demand is rising dramatically, outpacing historic trends
    •   Grid transformation and large loads warrant new engineering, planning, and operational
        requirements
    •   Extreme weather can impose broad, correlated stress
    •   Development of needed energy infrastructure faces execution risk

The long-term outlook shows widespread and worsening energy adequacy risk. As depicted in the chart
below, NERC’s 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (LTRA) finds that 13 of 23 assessment areas face
resource adequacy challenges over the next 10 years.



                                                      1
                         2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment – Risk Area Summary 2026–2030
             Shows highest risk classification that occurs in the first 5 years and states initial year of occurrence

Electricity peak demand and energy growth forecasts over the 10-year assessment period continue to climb
higher than at any point in the past two decades. Over the 10-year period, aggregated assessment area
summer peak demand is forecast to rise by over 224 GW. This is 69% higher than the 2024 10-year growth
projection of 132 GW. Winter peak demand is expected to grow by 245 GW, continuing to outpace summer
and exceed prior-year projections as more end-users turn to electricity for heating. New data centers, which
are inverter-based loads used for artificial intelligence and the digital economy, account for most of the
projected increase in North American electricity demand over the next 10 years. While NERC is working with
industry on reforms to account for these loads, the nature of their operations presents a paradigm shift.

Projections for resource and transmission growth lag what is needed to support new data centers, other
large loads, and electrification across sectors. Most new resources expected to come online in the next five
years consist of battery storage and solar photovoltaic (PV), which are inverter-based resources (IBRs) and
weather-dependent resources that increase the complexity of planning and operating a reliable grid.
Complexities include having adequate generation and energy storage to serve as balancing resources for
IBRs, and maintaining sufficient essential reliability services for voltage, frequency, and ramping needs.

Meanwhile, more fossil-fired generator retirements loom in the next five years, reducing the amount of
generation that has fuel on site and impacting the system’s ability to respond to spikes in demand. The LTRA
calls for mechanisms to extend service when needed for reliability and to align retirements with replacement
infrastructure. The objective is to maintain sufficient capability during the interval between an existing
plant’s decommissioning and replacement resource readiness.

In addition to documenting a shrinking conventional generator fleet, with a decline of 118 GW in on-peak
coal generator capacity over the past decade, the SOR identifies worsening performance. The report
identifies a meaningful increase in conventional generator forced outage rates in 2025, with annual weighted
                                                      2
 equivalent forced outage rates increasing to 9.2% compared to historical norms rarely exceeding 8%. Coal
and combined-cycle units were the primary drivers of this increase with an increase of over 39.8 TWh and
19.1 TWh of unavailable energy due to forced outages year over year, respectively.

The continuing shift in the resource mix toward weather-dependent resources and less fuel diversity
increases risks of supply shortfalls during winter months. As resource planners, market operators, and
regulators grapple with steep increases in demand and swelling resource queues, they face more
uncertainty, adding to the already complex endeavor of planning for resource adequacy during this period of
rapid grid transformation. To ensure there are sufficient resources for supplying electricity and needed
essential reliability services in the future to reliably meet the growing electricity needs for North Americans,
industry, regulators, and policymakers need to be vigilant for shifting projections, keep plans for deactivating
existing generators flexible, expedite system development, and perform robust adequacy and operational
reliability assessments of future scenarios. In addition, careful planning and broad cross-sector coordination
will be needed to navigate a period of potentially strained electricity resources.

Severe weather continues to stress the system across multiple days, regions, and fuel networks. The
September 2026 report, FERC, NERC, and Regional Entities, System Performance Review of the Winter 2026
Arctic Cold Period (Arctic Performance Review) identifies strong performance while cautioning underlying risk
factors. Extreme cold snaps persisted over extended days in parts of the Eastern and Texas Interconnections,
precipitating significant operational stresses on the electric and gas systems that require deliberate
attention. The report also finds strong system performance with no significant disruption to either system.
The report credits several factors, such as new cold weather reliability standards, leveraged insights from
past events, better coordination, advance fuel procurement, enhanced winter preparedness, and emergency
orders by the Secretary of Energy.

This winter showed that industry actions are making a difference; however, the work is not finished. Both the
electric and gas systems were stretched over multiple days, resulting in numerous reliability challenges that
continue to stress the system during extreme winter weather periods, increasing the potential for serious
reliability impacts. System operators relied on their full toolbox to keep the lights on. Multiple energy
emergencies were called. Such scenarios should not be considered the new normal. Winter brings significant
reliability risks, and energy systems remain highly interconnected.

The Arctic Performance Review found emergency orders by the Secretary of Energy assisted operators in
navigating the extreme cold snap periods this year. The preponderance of orders provided relief from
environmental emissions limits, while others addressed authority to direct data centers and other large load
backup resources to provide last resort generating support to maintain system reliability and deferred
retirement of limited generation. ISO-NE stated that the Secretary of Energy’s emergency order helped ISO-
NE maximize the availability of all generating resources in New England to meet expected demand for
electricity during the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period. PJM also emphasized the benefits of receiving an
emergency order from the Secretary of Energy. PJM stated it had 39 units with a total of 5,704 MW of
capacity that provided a total of 271,150 MWh of energy that would have otherwise been precluded from
operating without the emergency order. The emergency order also helped to provide operational certainty
necessary to purchase a multi-day block of natural gas over the first weekend of Winter Storm Fern. In the
South, FRCC stated that emergency orders enabled additional generation resources to remain available and
provided operational flexibility that supported grid reliability. While an emergency order can provide
meaningful help under certain circumstances, long-term, sustainable solutions are needed to address
resource adequacy challenges.


                                                       3
 The evolving resource mix and character, and large computational loads are changing the nature of
reliability risk, which must be addressed with urgency. Computational loads introduce unique operating
challenges beyond the resource adequacy concerns of planning for their electricity consumption. Their scale,
rapid development, inverter-based integration, and their interaction with the grid during normal operations,
and response to grid disturbances can affect system stability. For instance, NERC has documented a number
of events where over 1,000 megawatts of computational load unexpectedly disconnected in milliseconds to
seconds. These events risk compromising the system’s ability to maintain stable frequency and voltage. NERC
is working urgently on simultaneous fronts to address computational load risk. Initiatives include a Level 3
Alert to inform essential industry actions, a reliability guideline, criteria to register material computational
loads, and an initial set of foundational Reliability Standards to be filed with the Commission in 2026. NERC’s
Large Load Workplan and additional information on these activities are discussed in the section below
covering the topics for this conference.

Inverter-based resources, including solar, wind, and batteries, change the system’s dynamic response and its
requirements for modeling, protection, and disturbance ride-through. On May 15, 2026, NERC updated its
Compliance Registry to include identified entities that were registered as part of the IBR Registration
Initiative, completing Phase 3 of the FERC-approved work plan, closing a critical reliability gap, and advancing
ongoing efforts to identify, register, and support greater numbers of IBR owners and operators across North
America. NERC and the Regional Entities continue to identify and register additional entities that meet the
approved registration criteria and provide ongoing support. NERC has made substantial progress in
establishing Reliability Standards for IBRs, including gaps in disturbance performance, monitoring, data
sharing, and modeling. Collectively, these efforts support reliable integration and operation of IBRs,
harnessing the substantial reliability contributions of these resources.

NERC is also continuously scanning the horizon to identify and monitor risks, evaluating both recent events in
North America and throughout the globe where other jurisdictions are grappling with faster-paced resource
transformation. Evaluation of system performance indicates that the grid of the future must be smarter,
more adaptive, and significantly more resilient. The power system of the future will require reliability
standards that support fast-acting system strength and fast-acting control solutions, while simultaneously
accommodating electromechanical speed constraints.

Better forecasting of both demand and available resources is needed to strengthen planning and
operational readiness. Historic growth in demand for electricity illustrates some of the shortcomings in
forecasting such as when projects will connect, how quickly their consumption will grow, their ultimate size,
and their hourly operating patterns. Planners often lack reliable information about developers’
commitments, face multiple proposals for alternative locations, and have little historical experience with
these loads. In the current context, traditional forecasting methods are insufficient.

On the resource side, it is critical to assess when new generation will enter service and how much
dependable energy the resource mix can supply to all load during periods of stress. NERC is developing a
planning energy assurance reliability standard to help support this priority. The LTRA recommends
probabilistic methods – including effective load-carrying capability – to evaluate resource contributions,
alongside analysis of extreme weather, fuel limitations, and transmission constraints. NERC’s large-load
guidance also recommends testing delayed generation additions against different load-development
schedules and critically evaluating assumptions about demand response capability.



                                                       4
 NERC is addressing these issues through several concrete efforts. NERC’s large load guideline recommends
obtaining project information early, updating it throughout development, and considering tiers of
prospective load based on confidence in its size and timing. For operations, the guideline recommends that
large customers provide near-term demand forecasts, operating plans, telemetry, and advance notice of
substantial consumption changes. In NERC’s assessments work, enhancements include expanded energy
demand forecasts, revised categories to classify prospective generation, additional generator identification
and dual-fuel information, and expanded probabilistic assessment.

Faster generation and transmission additions are urgently needed. Even as studies demonstrate critical
need, timely development of new resources has been frustrated by legal, regulatory, and market constructs.
NERC applauds the Commission for pursuing nationwide interconnection reforms, changes to transmission
planning and permitting, and approving fast-track programs by RTOs and ISOs.

Regional initiatives to speed resource additions show considerable potential for meaningful progress. For
example, in April, NERC completed a sensitivity analysis concerning the risk profile for the Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region reflected in the LTRA. This analysis considered the successful
execution of new resource additions anticipated under MISO’s Expedited Resource Addition Study process.
This analysis incorporates approximately 25 GW of additional generation into the 2025 assessment
framework but does not reflect updated load growth projections or potential project delays, both key drivers
of reliability risk. Assuming these resources begin commercial operations as planned, risk in the MISO region
would fall to “normal” risk in 2028 through 2030. NERC is encouraged by these results and applauds MISO,
other ISO/RTOs, federal and state regulators for taking proactive action to expedite needed resources.

Timely addition of new resources that provide energy and essential reliability services is key to reducing
reliability risk. Expedited programs are critically important, however well-known legal, regulatory, and other
issues continue to present challenges that need to be addressed, including:

    •   Supply chain constraints affecting equipment delivery and construction timelines
    •   Transmission upgrades required for interconnection and deliverability
    •   Financing and cost allocation
    •   Natural gas pipeline and transportation limitations
    •   Regulatory and permitting delays


Panel 1: The State of Reliability in a Changing Energy Landscape - Operational Challenges of Integrating
Large Loads in Evolving System Dynamics

Introduction
NERC’s Large Loads Action Plan addresses the reliability challenges created by the rapid expansion of data
centers, artificial intelligence computing, cryptocurrency mining, and other large computational loads. The
initiative combines technical analysis, immediate risk mitigation, registration of qualifying computational load
entities, and development of Reliability Standards. Its scope encompasses both the challenges of
accommodating substantial new demand and the distinctive electrical behavior of these facilities, including
rapid consumption changes, oscillations, and simultaneous reductions in demand during grid disturbances.
NERC has advanced this work through incident reviews, technical conferences, industry outreach, and
successive alerts. In May 2026, NERC published a voluntary reliability guideline on mitigating emerging large
load risks and issued a Level 3 Essential Action Alert addressing computational load modeling, studies,
instrumentation, commissioning, operations, protection, and control. These efforts provide near-term
mitigation guidance while the development of reliability standards and registration processes proceed.
                                                       5
 Consistent with FERC’s directive, NERC will file registration criteria and foundational Reliability Standards
with the Commission before the end of 2026.

The Large Loads Working Group (LLWG) provides an ongoing forum for identifying, evaluating, and mitigating
reliability risks associated with large, complex, and rapidly evolving computational loads. Reporting to NERC’s
Reliability and Security Technical Committee (RSTC), its mission includes assessing emerging risks, supporting
analysis of actual disturbances, identifying weaknesses in industry practices and existing standards, and
developing technically justified mitigation proposals. Its scope includes computational loads and other
emerging industrial loads, such as hydrogen production facilities. The group develops white papers, technical
guidance, and Standard Authorization Requests, and supports the standards drafting process. Building on its
completed gap assessment and risk mitigation guideline, the LLWG examines disturbance performance,
appropriate simulation and study methods, and commissioning practices. It also coordinates with other NERC
groups and industry organizations to translate operating experience and technical research into practical
improvements in planning and operations.

The Load Modeling Working Group (LMWG), also reporting to the RSTC, has the complementary mission of
improving the development and use of dynamic load models across North America’s interconnections. These
models enable planners and operators to assess how electricity demand responds over time to disturbances
and changing system conditions. The group develops modeling guidance, data sets, technical references, and
educational resources. LMWG works with software vendors to achieve consistent model implementation
across simulation platforms and uses major system events to identify modeling deficiencies. Its
responsibilities extend across load types, including interactions with generation located behind customers’
meters. For data centers, the LMWG developed a technical reference, approved by the RSTC in July 2026, and
tools to help collect facility information needed for better models. This work supports more accurate studies
of computational load behavior and gives utilities, facility owners, manufacturers, and software developers a
common technical foundation.

NERC’s initial standards package under Project 2026-02 would establish three new foundational
computational load standards and revises two existing standards pertaining to the interconnection of new
facilities. The August 2026 proposed standard drafts generally apply to computational load sites with at least
50 MW of connected load supplied through equipment connected at 100 kV or above. The first
standard, CLO-001-1, Computational Load Interconnection, Studies, and Modeling Data, would require
documented interconnection requirements, coordinated studies of new facilities as well as qualifying
changes to existing facilities, and coordination of commissioning activities. It would establish responsibilities
for providing steady-state, short-circuit, and dynamic modeling information, including settings governing
disconnection, ride-through, and recovery after disturbances. Computational load owners would also provide
model verification while demonstrating that site-specific model parameters represent installed equipment as
well as settings and respond to technical concerns raised by planners.

The second proposed standard, CLO-002-1, Computational Load Operational Data and Communications,
would ensure that transmission operators, balancing authorities, and reliability coordinators obtain the
information needed for operational planning, monitoring, and reliability assessments. Computational load
owners and operators would satisfy specified data requirements. Computational load operators would
additionally maintain direct communications with grid operators, train personnel in receiving operating
instructions, and follow those instructions subject to defined physical, safety, equipment, and legal
limitations.

The third proposed standard, CLO-003-1, Computational Load Protection Coordination and Disturbance
Monitoring, would require coordination of protection settings with electrically connected facilities and
establish recording capabilities for breaker operations, faults, and dynamic disturbances. Requirements for
                                                       6
 synchronized measurements, data retention, and information sharing would give planners, operators, and
investigators the evidence needed to reconstruct events and assess facility performance.

Finally, changes to existing Reliability Standards, FAC-001, Facility Interconnection Requirements, and FAC-
002, Facility Interconnection Studies, are proposed to exclude computational load owners and operators to
avoid duplicative requirements with these existing standards. Together, these new standards and
modifications to the existing FAC standards will establish clearer responsibilities for operating coordination
and visibility into computational load behavior.

Heading into 2027, NERC’s work will build on these foundational requirements through additional standards
proposals addressing facility performance and system-wide adverse operating conditions. One priority for
standards development in 2027 includes voltage and frequency ride-through – the ability to remain
connected through specified disturbances – and the recovery of power consumption after faults. Another is
reporting unexpected facility operations and protection misoperations, conducting root-cause analysis,
developing mitigations, and establishing stronger requirements for dynamic model validation and model
quality assessment. A third is requiring planning and operational studies to evaluate the steady-state and
dynamic effects of clustered computational load losses, disconnections, and reconnections. These priorities
are reflected in the LLWG’s current workplan and Standard Authorization Requests under development.
Subsequent phases may also incorporate computational load requirements more broadly into existing
standards governing modeling, protection, interconnection, transmission planning, operations, reliability
coordination, and communications. As directed by the Commission, NERC will submit a workplan by March 1,
2027, identifying future phases of standards development.


Modeling and Planning Considerations, Lessons Learned from Integration of Large Loads (Topic 1)

The comparatively large size, unique end-use operational characteristics, unique facility design, and unique
operational performance of large loads necessitate enhancements to interconnection processes, BPS
planning studies and models, validation of installed facility equipment, and operational communication with
these customers. Accurate validated models, particularly dynamic models, of large loads are critical to
capture, assess, and mitigate the impact of large loads on the reliable operation of the BPS.

Entities should model and plan for these rapid advancements through careful engineering judgement,
reliance on known, workable processes, and development of new processes to set a standardized foundation
as seen in new Reliability Standards for these loads. Throughout NERC’s work concerning these new loads,
the need for technical procedures was highlighted as a major gap in the Level 2 Alert Large Load
Interconnection, Study, Commissioning, and Operations and Computational Load Modeling, Studies,
Instrumentation, Commissioning, Operations, Protection, and Control Level 3 Alert released in 2025 and
2026, respectively.

The findings from the Level 2 Alert demonstrated that entities largely did not have adequate procedures or
practices to handle the unique risk posed by computational load entities, including the necessary model
specification, data collection, model validation, and commissioning practices. The scale and timing of a
significant capacity of this load, as reported by Registered Entities in the Level 2 Alert, additionally raise
alarms that BPS reliability could be at stake. Furthermore, many reporting entities shared they are waiting on
action at a higher level, such as their ISO, RTO, or NERC to act to reliably integrate computational loads.
These findings underscore the ongoing work to finalize new and revised Reliability Standards to address
integration of computational load.



                                                      7
 As these procedures are critical to maintain BPS reliability, NERC sees this gap to be fully addressed in
revisions to its Reliability Standards, some coming by the end of 2026 and others planned for future
development. As an example, some key milestones to ensure high fidelity models are (1) providing the best
available equipment behavior during interconnection studies, (2) performing model validation, model
verification, model quality assessment, or a combination of these during commissioning of a facility, and (3)
ongoing performance assessment for operational computational load sites.


Advanced Grid Support Functions, Merits of Expanding ERCOT Example Nationwide (Topic 2)

Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are one technology type of the broader IBR classification that
addresses power electronic interfaced generation resources. This converter-coupled nature of IBR carries
with it a new way to model, study, and ensure the reliable performance of the BPS. Each technology has
strengths and weaknesses, and NERC has seen great applications of BESS resources in the System,
particularly for providing Essential Reliability Services (ERS). ERS are services that support the real power
delivery to end-use customers and cover a wide range of necessary, technical needs of the BPS for reliable
operations. BESS facilities in particular have demonstrated excellent performance-specific ERS based on their
operational profile. Some include frequency response, frequency control, or fast frequency response.
However, BESS facilities also can increase the risks posed by IBRs as they are converter-coupled and can carry
similar risks due to the power electronic interface. These stability risks were the focus of NERC’s recent
efforts to develop new and modified Reliability Standards in response to FERC Order 901. NERC’s response to
FERC Order 901 has included three years of standards development involving eight separate drafting teams
and fifteen new or modified Reliability Standards. Milestone 2 of Order 901 pertained to modifying system
protection and control standards to effectively address operational performance of IBR. Milestone 3 of Order
901 pertained to ensuring the development and coordination of adequate steady-state and dynamic models
of IBRs. Finally, Milestone 4 pertains to ensuring that operational and planning studies incorporate actual
performance and validated models for IBRs. Milestone 4 standards projects will be filed with FERC by the
November 4, 2026, deadline. As these new standards must be fully implemented by industry no later than
January 1, 2030, NERC has addressed specific stability concerns for all IBRs, including BESS facilities. With the
implementation of these standards, NERC continues to monitor the risk posed by all IBRs and is taking
appropriate action to ensure the reliable operation of the BPS.

Additionally, converter-coupled systems like computational loads have similar frequency, voltage, and
oscillatory stability risks. While the root causes of the stability risk are different between IBR and
computational load, the resulting impact and concerns are very similar due to their converter-coupled
nature. Given NERC’s strong effort in response to FERC Order 901 that strengthened its Reliability Standards
to address IBR risk and the ongoing work in Project 2026-02, NERC is well poised to ensure risks associated
with converter-coupled equipment are mitigated while allowing the strengths of all technology (BESS, Wind,
Solar PV, Gas, etc.) to be leveraged in the BPS.


Quantifying and Managing Declining System Inertia in Large Load Regions where Penetration is
Accelerating and Replacing Conventional Generation (Topic 3)

The Resources Subcommittee (RS) of NERC’s RSTC analyzes inertia trends in each interconnection on a
quarterly basis. In addition, many system operators monitor inertia in real-time. When inertia is low, tripping
of generators and loads cause frequency excursions to occur faster, leaving less time for generators to
provide frequency response. Some operators already quantify a “critical inertia” value. This value represents
the minimum inertia value that the system can tolerate the largest credible resource loss without activating
underfrequency load shed.
                                                       8
 One way to manage the risk posed by lower inertia (or inertia close to the “critical inertia” value) is to
increase the speed of primary frequency response to activate before the frequency nadir. This is also called
“fast frequency response” and the rapid injection of power during the arresting period increase the nadir and
the system-level performance for frequency excursions. Utilities should be considering ways to speed up the
frequency response as inertia declines to avoid activating underfrequency load shedding for credible losses in
their area. Entities should be cautious in how they speed up this performance. Many look to a reduction of
frequency droop. However, such a reduction can negatively impact the local stability margins while
improving the frequency nadir, so entities may need to manage lower inertia via a multifactored approach.

Inertia is not the only quantity that can describe the resistance to change brought on by IBRs replacing
conventional generators. “System strength” is one such quantity. This quantity helps to establish the relative
stability of a portion of the BPS compared to other areas and is indicative of potential poor reliability
performance that can lead to instability, cascading, or uncontrolled separation.

There are many different methods to quantify the available “system strength” in a local area. This quantity
helps establish the relative stability of a portion of the BPS compared to other areas and is indicative of
potential poor reliability performance that can lead to instability, cascading, or uncontrolled separation.
Operators should begin monitoring “system strength” as a metric, and industry should come to a stronger
consensus on which of the available methods are to be implemented. Some methods are:

    •   Short-circuit Ratio – Not well articulated for IBR dominated systems and doesn’t address locational
        aspects
    •   Equivalent Short Circuit Ratio – Addresses locational aspects, not well versed for IBR
    •   Inverter Penetration Short Circuit Ratio (IPSCR) – Assumes certain control of IBR, but computationally
        cheap in comparison and can address IBR dominated systems
    •   Impedance Margin Ratio (IMR) – Well versed for various IBR systems

While there are many other methods, not all result in the same value for this quantity. This can lead to other
performance risks. Accordingly, industry should come together and establish the method that will reliably
indicate potential poor performance and then implement that on the operating floor. And this needs to
become part of the power system planning approach, as assuming that enough inertia will be available with
the addition of generation is an assumption that no longer is valid.


Large Load Cybersecurity and Physical Security Risks (Topic 4)

Cyber and physical security of large loads are important issues warranting close attention and actions.
Emerging large loads are outside the scope of currently effective NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP)
Reliability Standards. As these facilities increasingly incorporate advanced control systems, behind-the-meter
generation, microgrids, and demand-side management capabilities, they introduce new cyberattack vectors
that may not be fully addressed by existing security requirements. Due to their significant scale and ability to
rapidly increase or decrease power consumption, cyber or physical compromises of these loads could
adversely affect the reliability of the Bulk Power System. However, one of the more important security risks
associated with large loads is the potential for a compromise of the systems that directly govern a
facility's electrical interaction with the grid. While varied systems may manage business-specific production

                                                       9
 workloads to influence demand at these facilities, today's reliability focus should be on the security of co-
located electrical OT assets and their associated industrial control systems. To address these emerging risks,
the NERC Security Integration and Technology Enablement Subcommittee (SITES) under the RSTC is
developing a white paper and a Standard Authorization Request to assess the security implications of
computational loads and determine what additional reliability and cybersecurity requirements are
warranted.


Accounting for Behind-the-Meter Gas-Fired Generators Compared to Front-of-Meter Gas-Fueled Power
Generators on the Same Pipeline (Topic 5)

Utilities have historically viewed the electrical impact of gas-fired generation facilities performance
independent of their available fuel supply. This is the norm as past generation facility had adequate energy
availability due to on-site fuel availability for their facility. In an era of pipeline disruptions and other mutual
outage modes (e.g., widespread impacts from weather), this assumption is challenged. Upon their effective
dates, FERC-approved standards BAL-007-1 and TOP-003-7 will require Balancing Authorities and
Transmission Operators to conduct energy reliability assessments, develop requisite Corrective Action Plans
for identified energy assurance deficiencies, and to implement those corrective actions.

These energy assessments rely on accurate data and models. Current models incorporate front-of-meter
data, while behind-the-meter generation (such as Distributed Energy Resources) relies on estimation
methods to establish their performance. Industry will need to improve their modeling and information
processes to mitigate the information availability between front-of-meter and behind-the-meter generation
when performing their energy assessments.


RTO/ISO Actions to Meet Capacity Requirements Through Secure Fuel Sources (Topic 6)

NERC does see potential energy assurance risks when the load profile(s) of load do not match up with the
deliverability of generation and transmission assets to serve them. Historically, these flatter load curves were
served by baseload generators that are aptly suited to meet this curve. Other structures can exist to reach
the same reliability objective. In all instances, the energy assessment of the deliverability of energy to load
should determine if a given asset fleet can meet the demands of the system.



Panel 2: Reliability in the West Under Drought Conditions

Introduction
Drought conditions have intensified across much of the Western Interconnection for the last two decades,
leading to aridification or the permanent, gradual change of a region's climate from wetter to drier. This can
result in more extreme weather events and worsening drought conditions, while also increasing the
hydrologic stress on rivers by lessening the amount of runoff available due to drier winters along with
increased evaporation and absorption into parched soil. A reduction of some hydro generation is a potential
result.

While drier conditions are not new to the West, drought conditions intensified this year after a below-
average snowpack was wiped out by an unusually warm spring. This brought record-low water levels to Lake
Powell and Lake Mead, which feed the two largest hydro projects on the Colorado River Basin. Glen Canyon
                                                  10
 and Hoover dams have a combined nameplate capacity of approximately 3.4 GW. At current water levels,
however, the two dams are generating at a fraction of capacity (1.1 GW). Earlier this year, the Bureau of
Reclamation warned Lake Powell could drop below minimum power pool level by August 2026 absent major
intervention. Action was taken to avoid that fate this year, but a healthy snowpack this winter is critical to
avoiding disruption at Glen Canyon and Hoover dams in 2027 — and to avoid risks to the water supply of
more than 40 million people.

Hydropower produces more electricity in the Western Interconnection than any other resource type except
natural gas. Although hydro comprises only 5% of the resource mix in the Southwest subregion, where Glen
Canyon and Hoover dams are located, it is 55% of the resource mix in the Pacific Northwest, where dozens of
dams are located on the Columbia and Snake rivers. Although winter 2026 brought wetter conditions to
much of the subregion, the state of Washington issued a drought declaration in spring 2026 for all
watersheds in the state due to the low snowpack and several years of lower-than-normal precipitation – the
first time that has happened. In Oregon, where the 2025-26 winter tied with 1934 as the warmest winter on
record, the governor has declared a drought emergency in 22 of the state's 36 counties. As aridification
progresses, the state expects to see more precipitation fall as rain than as snow, which could exacerbate
drought conditions and affect hydro generation in summer and fall 2027.

Hydro's ability to provide reliable baseload energy has made it a valuable cog in the resource mix in the
Western Interconnection, particularly as the resource mix has transformed in the last decade-plus from
thermal generation to more variable resources.

As drought conditions have persisted, WECC has collaborated with stakeholders to better understand and
mitigate the risks associated with the potential loss or curtailment of hydropower, to ensure we continue to
meet our mission of effectively and efficiently mitigating risks to the reliability and security of the bulk power
system.



Given Hydropower Resource Challenges in the Colorado River Basin, Preparation for Reliability in the
Short-Term and Long-Term Horizons (Topic 1)

WECC has warned for years that planned resource additions were not keeping pace with projected load
growth in the Western Interconnection. Based on the most recent resource plans, industry has heard our
pleas and is starting to act, with their plans signaling significant resource additions over the coming decade.
Resource plans filed this year indicate 271 GW of planned resource additions between 2027-2036. That is up
from 177 GW of capacity planned over the decade that was outlined in resource plans filed a year ago. For
context, 112 GW of installed capacity were added in the Western Interconnection between 2016-2025, and
the current interconnection-wide installed capacity is approximately 340 GW.

WECC has been in contact with the Western Area Power Administration and reviewed their studies regarding
resource loss in the Colorado River Basin to understand any resource adequacy, voltage, and/or frequency
concerns associated with ongoing and past drought. WECC will continue to collaborate with our stakeholders
to maintain awareness of and mitigate any reliability risks associated with the aridification of the West.

WECC’s upcoming Western Assessment of Resource Adequacy examines the near-term impact of the loss
and/or curtailment of hydro across the Western Interconnection, including Glen Canyon and Hoover dams.
Although our analysis is not complete, preliminary findings indicate there would be minimal impact on
resource adequacy if these generating resources were unavailable. As mentioned, while their nameplate

record-low water levels in Lakes Mead and Powell. This preliminary finding coincides with the findings of a

Needed Changes to Resource Adequacy Planning Models in Light of Uncertainty Related to Hydropower
Generation, Large Loads Additions, and the Transformation of the Resource Mix (Topic 2)
Given the aridification of the West, it is imperative for entities within the Western Interconnection to
consider drought scenarios in their resource adequacy and energy sufficiency assessments. Adjustments to
modeling assumptions could range from curtailed hydro generation due to low reservoir levels to more
complex interactions such as modeling reservoir volumes and reservoir replenishment rates, aligning
streamflow forecasts with run-of-river hydro capability, and derating pumped storage facilities.

The Department of Energy's national laboratories are also working to assist industry in hydro modeling
efforts. The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory is developing a dashboard that correlates streamflow
forecasts with hydro generation output, for example, and the National Laboratory of the Rockies has
developed the Climate Water and Risk Assessment Tool (CWRAT), which pairs climate models with hydro
conditions and electric power sector impacts, and may have applications in long-term planning studies.

In general, as the transformation of the resource mix continues in the Western Interconnection, the certainty
of energy availability for any given hour decreases. The decline of reliable hydro generation in the Colorado
River Basin only adds to this uncertainty.

There is also significant uncertainty surrounding large load interconnection requests. WECC's collaboration
with entities across the interconnection has revealed numerous methods for hedging these load forecasts
given their speculative nature.

Considering the uncertain nature of factors on both sides of the equation (supply and demand), probabilistic
resource adequacy models that examine a wide range of possible conditions and scenarios, both
independently and in tandem, are a necessity moving forward.



Reliability Planning Frameworks for the West – Most Significant Risk and Mitigation (Topic 3)

The most significant risk in reliability planning frameworks for the Western Interconnection is the ability to
accurately forecast, model, and represent key assumptions (hydrological conditions and load forecasts, for
example) amid the rapid transformation of the resource mix. While one faulty assumption might not have a
significant impact, multiple inaccuracies compound the risk to the Bulk Power System. At the same time, it
has likely never been more difficult to develop accurate forecasts with more extreme weather events and
uncertainty surrounding large loads, while the changing characteristics of the resource mix add complexity.
WECC has made strides to mitigate this risk in recent years, working with the entities to improve our
forecasting and modeling efforts. Continued and enhanced collaboration and communication with our
stakeholders will be critical for addressing this risk.

WECC’s mission is to effectively and efficiently mitigate risks to the reliability and security of the Bulk Power

economics would be better addressed by organizations focused on those uses.


Integrating Rapidly Shifting Hydrological Forecasts into Multi-Year Planning Processes (Topic 5)
Entities in the West have done a commendable job incorporating extreme weather events (heat and cold) in
their resource and transmission planning efforts. We recommend taking the additional step of including
water shortage conditions to these scenarios. Several resources are available to assist in this effort, including
the hydro modeling work underway at the national laboratories that was mentioned in the answer to
Question 2. WECC will continue to raise awareness of this reliability risk, and to collaborate with our
stakeholders to address it.



Western Entities Prepare for Compounding Reliability Risks Including Hydropower Shortages, Extreme
Heat, Conventional Generation Limitations Due to Cooling Shortages, Conventional Generator
Retirements, Reduced Natural Gas Supplies, and Significant Load Growth (Topic 6)

WECC is working with stakeholders through our recently updated Risk Management Program to identify and
mitigate reliability risks associated with these compounding stresses. We are also performing several
scenarios examining compound elements of risk in the upcoming Western Assessment of Resource
Adequacy, including a scenario examining the impact of near-term drought conditions in tandem with the
integration of large load customers and a reduction in generation resource additions. The objective is to
bring attention to these issues and provide entities in the West with a forum and resources for mitigating
risks to reliability. Armed with the knowledge of how compounding risks can impact the broader
interconnection, the individual entities can use WECC's resources to further examine the risks to reliability
while developing unique solutions for mitigating the risks — solutions that could range from thermal
resource repower or life extension, additional resource acquisition, transmission expansion (more of a long
term solution), to the roll out of new controllable demand response programs.

From a planning perspective, there is a dearth of data linking thermal resource availability to drought
conditions. Information on the impacts of water availability on thermal generation is often location-specific,
making it difficult to develop an accurate, interconnection-wide representation. Drought projections in the
mid-term are also difficult to find. While there are numerous climate models for 10 years out and longer, and
the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation publishes monthly forecasts for two years out, it is difficult to find recently
updated forecasts between 3-10 years out.

From an operations perspective regarding overall river/reservoir operations, information related to
forecasted, scheduled, and real-time data is provided to the operators to ensure the safe, reliable operation
of river systems/reservoirs, dams, and electrical aspects of power plants. Operationally, the various operating
entities share datasets and coordinate river/reservoir operations in a forward timeframe and through real-
time operations. Considering a constant improvement approach as system conditions change, a review of the
current datasets, and shared visibility may be beneficial among the operating entities.
